If clinically suspected, the diagnosis can be confirmed with brain MRI. C

background.definition: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) is a subacute or rapidly advancing dymelinating disorder of the CNS that effects many different areas in the brain only (sparing the spinal cord or optic nerve).

list.listitem: HIV positive patients: incidence in Africa is 1.5% versus 4% to 10% in Europe and the USA.

In MS patients treated with natalizumab, the risk is estimated to be 1 person for every 1,000 patients treated for 18 months. However, a more recent independent review of postmarketing data condluded that in patients who are JCV positive and who previously used immunosuppressants, the incidence of PML after 2 to 4 years of natalizaumab is 20 per 1000. It is lower in patients who had not used immunosuppressants, at 7 per 1000.
Medication-associated PML has become an increasingly common, although still rare
Efalizumab (Raptiva) increased risk of PML and was removed from US and European markets in June of 2009. A
A French study found a population incidence of 0.11 per 100,000 person-years.
There has been one documented case in a patient without known risk factors.
JC (John Cunningham) virus, a polyomavirus infection of oligodendrocytes and astrocytes in the brain, usually in immunocompromised individuals.
Risk is greatest in patients taking natalizumab, but is also increased with other iatrogenic immunosuppression.
JC virus brain infection is very common; prevalence is up to 50% in children age 10 years.
Virus is intermittently shed in urine in patients who are infected.
Virus is believed to remain latent in kidneys, tonsils, bone marrow,other lymphoid tissue, and brain tissue.
The JC virus must be present and become activated. PML may then develop slowly for months to years until rapid decline in cognition and death.
In patients with HIV infection with immunocompromise, the infection progresses.
Other factors may include hematologic malignancies and iatrogenic (drug) immune suppression, with monoclonal antibodies, dimethyl fumarate, or fingolimod.
Testing positive for JC virus antibodies in patient treated with natalizumab is a risk factor for PML. C
There is no known way to prevent a primary JC virus infection.
In a patient with progressive neurologic symptoms without optic neuritis or spinal cord involvement, perform a complete neurologic exam. C
Brain MRI is key to diagnosis. C
PCR of cerebrospinal fluid for JC virus offers additional confirmation. C
HIV testing is important if PML is suspected. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Usually one presenting symptom in MS; optic nerve or spinal cord involvement rules out PML
Dementia, depression are typical presenting symptoms
CSF testing with cytology, MRI of the brain appears different
age 15 to 25, HIV negative, responsive to steroids, rapid progression
CSF hemorrhagic, HSV PCR, classic temporal lobe findings on MRI

list.listitem: The most common symptoms are persistent and progressive gait disorders (54%), limb weakness (43%), speech disorders (41%), altered mental status (31%), and visual symptoms (26%).

Signs may include hemiparesis or monoparesis (42-46%), weakness, including ataxia (33%), and dysmetria (26%), visual deficits (45%), typically a homonymous hemianopia (24%-26%), and altered mental status (19%-38%) (including dementia or personality change, although dementia alone is not a common finding).
Patients do not have spinal cord symptoms or optic neuritis.
PML may be confused with multiple sclerosis.
In some cases, PML may be the presenting AIDS-defining infection in persons with HIV infection.

Brain MRI: Should be read by neuroradiologist as other neurologic processes maybe confused with PML. There is no clinical correlation between the brain MRI lesion appearance and the severity of the clinical presentation. In rare cases of improvement, MRI findings may lag behind clinical improvement by 1 month.

A positive CSF PCR test for JC virus is almost 100% specific, with a sensitivity greater than 90%. A negative test cannot rule out PML, and it should not be the primary means to diagnose, but it can support the diagnosis of PML. The PCR test may not be readily available and sensitivity may vary among tests. Brain biopsy and autopsy. can also support a diagnosis but are obviously not be the primary means to diagnose PML.
If HIV status unknown in a patient with PML without other known immunosuppression, the patient should be tested for HIV.

JCV testing of serum and urine is unlikely to help predict PML development in patients treated with natalizumab or in HIV positive patients C but antibody positive patients treated with natalizumab are at higher risk of developing PML.
In an immunocompromised patient with the new onset of neurologic signs and symptoms suggestive of PML, perform a complete neurologic evaluation.
If clinically suspected, obtain a brain MRI and refer to a neurologist.
PCR of serum and CSF for JC virus can also help confirm the diagnosis.
Treatment is largely supportive, although HAART may lengthen survival in HIV patients.
Treatment of HIV positive patients with HAART may prolong survival. B
It is unknown if discontinuation of iatrogenic immunosuppression for MS affects PML progression, but standard of care would be to discontinue all immunosuppressing medications. C
Treatment of PML induced by rituximab or natalizumab includes discontinuing the drug and initiating plasma exchange. C
Mirtazipine may benefit autoimmune/rheumatic disease (ARD)-associated PML mortality, but not HIV related PML. Evidence is very limited. C
There is no known effective treatment for the JC virus, the causative factor in PML.
IV cidofovir is not effective.
HAART in HIV positive patients may prolong survival in PML. This is based primarily on observational data in the absence of clinical trials.
A systematic review identified 5 cohort studies and 74 case reports. The cohort studies found no evidence of benefit for mirtazapine.
A trial of 57 patients with HIV associated PML found that cyarabine was not effective. A second study found that mefloquine was also not effective.
A case series of 8 patients treated with pembrolizumab found some measures of clinical and virological improvement in 5 of 8.

A poor quality retrospective chart review found increased survival with alpha-interferon, but proper clinical trials are needed. A small case series found some potential for treatment with topotecan, but as with alpha-interferon, additional studies are required.
Discontinuation of immunosuppression may lead to an immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome.
Supportive care is the primary treatment.
Treatment of PML induced by rituximab or natalizumab includes discontinuing the drug and initiating plasma exchange.
A review of the literature found no evidence to support the use of plasmapheresis in patients with PML associated with the use of natalizumab.
Patients with suspected PML should be referred to a neurologist.
Patients with suspected PML should be admitted for supportive care, along with MRI brain, and further exams such as lumbar puncture as directed by a neurologist.
PML is usually fatal, typically within 14-64 weeks in HIV positive patients but HAART may prolong survival.
The usual natural course of PML if untreated is progressive cognitive decline. The patient eventually enters a persistent comatose state and leading to death.
The prognosis for patients whose PML is associated with MS and natalizumab treatment appears to be better than in HIV associated PML.
A report of 326 cases of drug associated PML found that 52% died during follow-up, which was of variable duration.
